name: ACCG-2671

angle.text: ACCG-2671 is an early oral amylin agonist for obesity that appears in pipeline-watching fat-loss discussion. Its only public record is a first-in-human trial registration, so its weight-loss effect has not been shown.

summary: An early-stage oral amylin agonist for obesity known only from a single first-in-human trial registration.
note: No published results; not approved.
currentQuick:
ACCG-2671 is an experimental oral amylin agonist being tested for obesity. It is at the very first stage of human testing.
No results have been published, so nothing is known publicly about its effect on weight.
How it works: It is described as a small-molecule amylin receptor agonist taken by mouth; amylin agonists are studied for effects on satiety.
Risks and caveats: Safety and tolerability are the subject of the ongoing first-in-human trial; no data are public. It is not approved.
deepLead:
ACCG-2671 is an investigational oral small-molecule amylin receptor agonist being studied for obesity. The only public record of it is a registered first-in-human phase 1/2 trial examining its safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and the effect of food. 
No results have been published. Amylin agonists are a class of weight-management candidates that act on satiety pathways, but information specific to this compound is limited to the trial registration.

name: Elecoglipron

angle.text: Elecoglipron is AstraZeneca's once-daily GLP-1 pill, followed by fat-loss communities for its convenience and phase 2 weight loss of up to about 10% at 26 weeks. Phase 3 is under way, and appearance-focused outcomes have not been studied.

summary: AstraZeneca's once-daily oral GLP-1 pill, with up to about 10% weight loss at 26 weeks in phase 2 and phase 3 now under way.
note: Investigational and not approved.
currentQuick:
Elecoglipron is an experimental oral GLP-1 agonist from AstraZeneca, taken once daily as a tablet with no food or fluid restrictions.
In a phase 2 obesity trial, average weight loss at 26 weeks reached 10.5% at the top dose versus 0.6% on placebo. A phase 2b diabetes trial showed HbA1c reductions up to 1.88 points.
How it works: It activates the GLP-1 receptor, the pathway used by semaglutide, but as a small-molecule non-peptide that can be swallowed.
Risks and caveats: Adverse events were mainly gastrointestinal: nausea, constipation, diarrhoea, headache and vomiting. Phase 3 trials are ongoing and it is not approved.
deepLead:
Elecoglipron (AZD5004, also ECC5004) is an investigational oral, small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by AstraZeneca for weight management and type 2 diabetes. It is taken as a once-daily tablet without food or fluid restrictions. 
In a 36-week phase 2 trial in adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes (VISTA), mean weight change at week 26 ranged from -2.6% to -10.5% across dose groups versus -0.6% on placebo. In a phase 2b trial in type 2 diabetes (SOLSTICE), HbA1c fell by 0.91 to 1.88 percentage points versus 0.15 on placebo. Common adverse events were gastrointestinal. 
It is not approved. A large phase 3 programme in obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease began in mid-2026.

name: AZD6234

angle.text: AZD6234 is AstraZeneca's long-acting amylin agonist injection for obesity, noted in fat-loss pipeline discussion. Phase 3 is registered but no efficacy results are published, so its weight-loss effect is untested in public data.

summary: AstraZeneca's weekly-style amylin agonist injection for obesity, with phase 3 registered but no published efficacy results.
note: Investigational; no published trial results found.
currentQuick:
AZD6234 is an experimental injectable amylin agonist from AstraZeneca being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Phase 3 trials were registered in 2026, but no efficacy results have been published.
How it works: It mimics amylin, a satiety hormone that acts on the brain and slows glucagon release after meals. It is also being tested together with AZD9550.
Risks and caveats: Safety is being assessed in phase 1 and 3 studies; no published adverse-event data were found. It is not approved.
deepLead:
AZD6234 is an investigational long-acting selective amylin receptor agonist developed by AstraZeneca for obesity and type 2 diabetes, given by subcutaneous injection. 
Amylin is a hormone co-secreted with insulin that acts centrally to promote satiety. The first amylin-based drug, pramlintide, found limited use as an add-on to insulin, and longer-acting analogues are now being developed for weight loss.  No results from AZD6234 trials have been published in the sources reviewed here; its evidence is limited to early-phase registrations, with phase 3 trials registered from 2026.

name: AZD9550

angle.text: AZD9550 is an experimental GLP-1/glucagon dual agonist from AstraZeneca, discussed by fat-loss followers because glucagon activity is linked to extra calorie burn. It is tested alone and with an amylin agonist, with no published results yet.

summary: AstraZeneca's experimental GLP-1/glucagon injection, tested alone and with an amylin agonist, with no published results yet.
note: Investigational; no published trial results found.
currentQuick:
AZD9550 is an experimental injectable drug that activates both GLP-1 and glucagon receptors, developed by AstraZeneca for obesity.
It has been through phase 1 and phase 2 trials, including a combination with AZD6234, but no results have been published.
How it works: GLP-1 activation reduces appetite, while glucagon receptor activation is intended to add effects on energy use and the liver. This is as described by the compound class; no AZD9550-specific data are public.
Risks and caveats: No published safety data were found. It is not approved and is only available in clinical trials.
deepLead:
AZD9550 is an investigational GLP-1/glucagon receptor dual agonist from AstraZeneca, given by subcutaneous injection and studied for obesity and related liver disease. 
Evidence is limited to early-phase trial registrations. Phase 1 and phase 2 studies have tested it alone and in combination with AZD6234, an amylin agonist; no results from these trials have been published in the sources reviewed.

name: Berobenatide

angle.text: Berobenatide is Pfizer's investigational monthly GLP-1 agonist, noted in fat-loss pipeline discussion for its dosing frequency. Only phase 3 registrations exist, so its weight-loss effect is untested in public data.

summary: Pfizer's investigational monthly GLP-1 agonist for obesity; only Phase 3 registrations exist so far.
note: Unapproved investigational drug; no published results.
currentQuick:
Berobenatide is an experimental GLP-1 receptor agonist from Pfizer, aimed at weight management. It is not approved for any use.
The public record consists of two Phase 3 trial registrations, in sleep apnea and in stress urinary incontinence, each in people with overweight or obesity. No results have been published.
How it works: As a GLP-1 receptor agonist it is expected to act like other drugs in the class, which reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying. The registry describes monthly dosing.
Risks and caveats: Safety in humans has not been published. It is an unapproved investigational drug and not available through legitimate prescribing.
deepLead:
Berobenatide (also written PF-08653944 and MET-097i) is an investigational long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist being developed by Pfizer for weight management. It is not approved anywhere and has no appearance-related indication. Information available publicly is limited to clinical trial registrations.
Two Phase 3 trials are listed on ClinicalTrials.gov: one in adults with obstructive sleep apnea and overweight or obesity who use a PAP machine, which describes the drug as given monthly, and one in women with stress urinary incontinence and overweight or obesity. No results from these trials have been published.

name: PF-08653945

angle.text: PF-08653945 is Pfizer's early-stage amylin analogue for weight management, appearing in fat-loss pipeline discussion. Nothing has been published on its effects, so its link to leanness is untested.

summary: Pfizer's early-stage amylin analogue for obesity; nothing published on it yet.
note: Investigational only; no human data found.
currentQuick:
PF-08653945 is an experimental amylin analogue being developed for weight loss. No trials or results were found for it specifically.
Amylin analogues are a drug class reviewed in 2026 as a possible next step after GLP-1 drugs.
How it works: Amylin analogues mimic a pancreatic hormone involved in satiety and slowing of digestion.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data for this compound are not public. It is unapproved and not legitimately available.
deepLead:
PF-08653945 (also MET-233i) is an investigational amylin analogue for weight management, listed as being developed by Pfizer. It is not approved and has no published human trial results in the sources reviewed.
It belongs to the amylin analogue class, which a 2026 narrative review describes as an emerging therapeutic approach to obesity complementing incretin-based drugs.

name: ABBV-295

angle.text: ABBV-295 is AbbVie's injectable amylin analogue for obesity, noted in fat-loss pipeline discussion. It is in early trials with no results out, so its weight-loss effect is untested in public data.

summary: AbbVie's injectable amylin analogue for obesity, now in early trials with no results out.
note: Investigational; Phase 1-2 only.
currentQuick:
ABBV-295 is an experimental amylin analogue injected under the skin, developed by AbbVie for obesity.
Registered trials include several Phase 1 studies and a Phase 2 trial of about 360 adults. No results are public.
How it works: Amylin analogues mimic the hormone amylin, which promotes satiety and slows gastric emptying.
Risks and caveats: Safety data are not published. The drug is unapproved.
deepLead:
ABBV-295 (also GUB014295) is an investigational amylin analogue given by subcutaneous injection, being developed by AbbVie for obesity. It is not approved.
Registered trials include Phase 1 studies in adults with obesity, in Japanese participants with overweight or obesity, and in women taking oral contraceptives, and a Phase 2 trial in 360 adults with obesity or overweight and weight-related comorbidities that began recruiting in August 2026. No results have been published. A registered psoriasis study lists targeted therapies and is not described as an ABBV-295 efficacy trial.

name: Pramlintide

angle.text: Pramlintide is an approved diabetes drug that fat-loss circles discuss because weight loss appears alongside its blood sugar effects and it is an amylin analogue like newer obesity drugs. Weight loss was observed in diabetes trials; use for cosmetic leanness is off-label.

summary: Approved amylin analogue for insulin-treated diabetes; weight loss is a side-effect signal, not an approved use.
note: Boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia with insulin.
currentQuick:
Pramlintide is an injectable copy of amylin, approved in 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in diabetes. Trials found small improvements in blood sugar and weight loss rather than gain.
It is not approved for obesity. Obesity research on it centres on combinations such as with metreleptin.
How it works: It slows stomach emptying, reduces glucagon after meals and increases satiety.
Risks and caveats: The label has a boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia when used with insulin. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Pramlintide (brand name Symlin) is a synthetic analogue of amylin, a hormone released by pancreatic beta cells with insulin. The US FDA approved it in March 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who have not reached glucose targets. It is injected subcutaneously.
Amylin slows gastric emptying, promotes satiety and reduces glucagon secretion. In trials of insulin-treated patients, pramlintide lowered HbA1c modestly and was associated with weight loss rather than the weight gain typical of insulin. Its weight effect has been studied in obesity research, including in combination with metreleptin, but it is not approved for obesity. Its US label carries a boxed warning for severe hypoglycemia when used with insulin.

name: Dulaglutide

angle.text: Dulaglutide is a weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug that some fat-loss followers view as an older relative of semaglutide, taken for lower appetite and modest weight loss. Weight loss was seen in diabetes trials; it is not approved for obesity.

summary: Weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug with proven cardiovascular benefit and modest weight loss; not approved for obesity.
note: Boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors (rodents).
currentQuick:
Dulaglutide is a once-weekly GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood sugar, reduced cardiovascular events in the REWIND trial and causes modest weight loss.
A head-to-head trial found semaglutide produced larger weight and HbA1c reductions.
How it works: It activates GLP-1 receptors, raising insulin release when glucose is high, slowing stomach emptying and reducing appetite.
Risks and caveats: Common effects are nausea and diarrhea. A boxed warning covers thyroid C-cell tumors in rats; pancreatitis is also warned. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Dulaglutide (brand name Trulicity) is a once-weekly injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist made by Eli Lilly for type 2 diabetes. It consists of GLP-1 linked to a fragment of human IgG4 antibody, extending its duration of action. The FDA approved it in September 2014 and the EU in November 2014.
Beyond glucose control, it is labelled to reduce major cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease or multiple risk factors, based on the REWIND trial. It also causes modest weight loss, but it is not approved for weight management. The US label carries a boxed warning on thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents.

name: Lixisenatide

angle.text: Lixisenatide is a short-acting daily GLP-1 diabetes drug that appears in fat-loss discussion mainly as an older member of the GLP-1 class. Small weight reductions were seen in diabetes trials, and it plays a minor role compared with newer agents.

summary: Short-acting daily GLP-1 diabetes drug, cardiovascular-neutral in ELIXA; minor role in weight loss.
note: Not approved for obesity; largely superseded by longer-acting agents.
currentQuick:
Lixisenatide is a daily GLP-1 injection for type 2 diabetes, approved in the EU in 2013 and US in 2016. ELIXA showed neutral cardiovascular outcomes.
It is also sold in a combination with insulin glargine.
How it works: It activates GLP-1 receptors, boosting insulin release when glucose is high and slowing gastric emptying.
Risks and caveats: Nausea and vomiting are common; pancreatitis and allergic reactions are rarer. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Lixisenatide (Lyxumia in the EU, Adlyxin in the US) is a once-daily injectable short-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes, developed by Zealand Pharma and licensed to Sanofi in 2003. It was approved in the EU in February 2013 and in the US in July 2016.
In the ELIXA trial of patients with type 2 diabetes and a recent acute coronary event, it did not increase cardiovascular events relative to placebo. Its weight effect is modest and it is not approved for obesity. It is also marketed combined with insulin glargine as Soliqua.

name: Albiglutide

angle.text: Albiglutide is a withdrawn weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug that fat-loss readers sometimes cite as an early member of the GLP-1 family behind newer weight-loss injections. Its weight effects in diabetes trials were modest, and it was never studied as an appearance or cutting tool.

summary: A withdrawn once-weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug; it was never a weight-loss product and produced modest weight effects in trials.
note: No longer marketed anywhere; approved only for type 2 diabetes.
currentQuick:
Albiglutide was a weekly injection for type 2 diabetes in the same drug class as semaglutide and liraglutide. It was approved in 2014 and pulled from the market by GSK in 2017-2018 for commercial reasons.
It was never licensed for weight loss, and published comparisons rate its weight and blood-sugar effects as smaller than those of other drugs in its class.
How it works: It is a modified GLP-1 fused to albumin, which resists breakdown and lasts about five days in the body. It activates GLP-1 receptors, which raises insulin release after meals, lowers glucagon and slows stomach emptying.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include nausea, diarrhoea and injection-site reactions, with pancreatitis uncommon. The label carried a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumours seen in rodent studies of the class. It is no longer sold.
deepLead:
Albiglutide (brand names Tanzeum in the United States and Eperzan in Europe) is a once-weekly injectable glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist that was approved to improve blood-sugar control in adults with type 2 diabetes. It was developed by Human Genome Sciences and marketed by GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) .
It is a fusion protein made of two copies of a modified human GLP-1 sequence attached to human albumin, a design that slows its breakdown and lets it be dosed weekly . It was approved in Europe in March 2014 and in the US in April 2014, and GSK announced a worldwide withdrawal in 2017 for economic reasons .
Albiglutide was never approved for weight loss. It appears in a looksmaxxing-adjacent wiki because it belongs to the GLP-1 class of drugs that has become prominent in fat-loss discussions. Trials in diabetes reported modest weight effects, and a 2015 analysis cited on Wikipedia found it less effective than other GLP-1 agonists on both blood-sugar and weight measures .

name: Peptide YY

angle.text: Peptide YY is a gut hormone released after meals, and users interested in appetite control discuss it as a natural fullness signal that could support dieting toward a leaner physique. Infusion studies show reduced food intake; use for appearance is untested and it is not an established tool.

summary: A satiety hormone made in the gut; infusion studies show reduced intake, but it is not an approved or established appearance tool.
note: No approved PYY drug exists; evidence is from small studies.
currentQuick:
Peptide YY is a hormone your gut releases after you eat, signalling fullness. The 2002 and 2003 studies that showed it cut food intake sparked interest in using it for weight control.
It remains a research compound. Human studies are small and short, and no PYY product is approved for weight loss.
How it works: The active form, PYY(3-36), binds Y2 receptors, including on appetite-regulating neurons in the hypothalamus, and also slows stomach emptying. Levels rise with meals, especially protein-rich ones.
Risks and caveats: Published material here does not detail safety outcomes of PYY analogues; research use is investigational and no regulatory approval for weight management exists.
deepLead:
Peptide YY (PYY) is a 36-amino-acid gut hormone released by L-cells in the ileum and colon after eating. It acts to reduce appetite and slow gastric emptying, and it belongs to the neuropeptide Y family . The main circulating form, PYY(3-36), acts largely through the Y2 receptor .
In 2002, researchers reported in Nature that peripheral injection of PYY(3-36) reduced food intake in rodents and in human volunteers, which led to interest in it as an anti-obesity agent . It is not an approved drug for weight management or appearance. Research is described as investigational, with some small human infusion studies and an oral/lingual delivery trial registered .

name: ACE-031

angle.text: ACE-031 is an experimental myostatin-blocking protein that muscle-focused forum users cite as a route to growth beyond natural limits. It was tested in healthy women and boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, where it raised muscle measures; physique use in healthy lifters is untested and the trials ended.

summary: An experimental myostatin-blocking fusion protein tested in healthy women and Duchenne boys; trials ended and it is not approved.
note: Unapproved; Duchenne trials were terminated.
currentQuick:
ACE-031 is a lab-made decoy receptor designed to soak up myostatin and similar proteins that restrain muscle growth. It was tested for muscle-wasting disease.
It never reached approval, and anti-doping scientists have published detection methods for black-market versions.
How it works: It is a fusion of the activin receptor IIB with an antibody Fc piece. It binds myostatin and related ligands in the blood so they cannot signal in muscle.
Risks and caveats: The healthy-volunteer study reported it generally well tolerated, with injection-site reactions. The Duchenne trials were terminated, and it is unapproved.
deepLead:
ACE-031 is a soluble fusion protein of the activin receptor type IIB (ActRIIB) and the Fc part of IgG1. It acts as a decoy that binds myostatin and related ligands that limit muscle growth .
It was developed for muscle-wasting conditions and tested in healthy postmenopausal women and in boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy . The Duchenne trials were terminated . It is not approved anywhere. Analytical chemists have published methods for detecting black-market ACE-031, indicating interest from athletes outside clinical settings .

name: Stamulumab

angle.text: Stamulumab is a discontinued antibody against myostatin that muscle-minded readers mention as an early attempt at removing the body's growth brake. It was tested in muscular dystrophy rather than for physique, so appearance use in healthy people is untested.

summary: A discontinued Wyeth antibody that blocks myostatin; tested in muscular dystrophy, never approved or studied for physique.
note: Development abandoned in 2008; not available.
currentQuick:
Stamulumab was one of the first antibodies designed to block myostatin, the protein that restrains muscle growth. Wyeth tested it in healthy volunteers and in adults with muscular dystrophy.
The company stopped developing it for muscular dystrophy in 2008, and it has never been studied for appearance.
How it works: It binds myostatin in the blood so the protein cannot activate its receptor on muscle cells.
Risks and caveats: Published sources reviewed here do not detail its safety results. It is an unapproved, discontinued investigational antibody.
deepLead:
Stamulumab (MYO-029) is an experimental monoclonal antibody that binds myostatin, a protein that limits muscle growth. It was developed by Wyeth as a possible treatment for muscular dystrophy .
It was tested in a phase 1 study in healthy volunteers and a phase 1/2 trial in adults with several muscular dystrophies . Wyeth announced on 11 March 2008 that it would not continue developing it for muscular dystrophy . It was never approved, and no study has examined it for cosmetic muscle building.

name: ARO-INHBE

angle.text: ARO-INHBE is an experimental RNAi drug that fat-loss followers watch because it targets fat distribution rather than appetite, with the hope of a leaner waistline. It is in early obesity trials only; its effect on appearance is untested and no results are available.

summary: An experimental RNAi drug against INHBE aimed at fat distribution; only early trial registrations exist so far.
note: Investigational only; no published human results.
currentQuick:
ARO-INHBE is an experimental RNA interference drug that targets the INHBE gene. It is in early clinical trials for obesity and is planned for a trial in fatty liver disease (MASH).
No results have been published, so its effects on fat, weight or muscle in people are unknown.
How it works: RNAi drugs reduce the production of a specific protein by silencing its gene. Here the target is INHBE, a gene linked to how fat is distributed in the body.
Risks and caveats: Safety in humans has not been reported. The drug is investigational and not available by prescription.
deepLead:
ARO-INHBE is an investigational RNA interference (RNAi) therapy aimed at the INHBE gene, which encodes a liver-derived protein involved in fat distribution. It is being tested in people with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes, and in a planned trial in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). It is not approved for any use anywhere.
The only public information about the compound is its clinical trial registrations. A first-in-human Phase 1/2 study in adults with obesity began in December 2024 and is active but no longer recruiting, with an enrollment of 190. A Phase 2 MASH trial of 252 adults is registered as not yet recruiting, with a start date of September 2026. No results have been posted in the sources reviewed.
Interest in INHBE-targeting drugs in appearance communities centres on the idea of reducing fat while preserving muscle, a theme discussed for other drugs in the same class. No published human data on ARO-INHBE show whether it does this.

name: ARO-ALK7

summary: An experimental RNAi drug against ALK7 for obesity; a single early trial is recruiting and no results exist.
note: Investigational only; no published human data.

ARO-ALK7 is an experimental RNA interference drug aimed at the ALK7 gene, being tested for obesity in a first-in-human trial.
No results have been published, so its effects are unknown.
How it works: RNAi drugs lower production of a chosen protein by silencing its gene; here the target is ALK7.

deepLead:
ARO-ALK7 is an investigational RNA interference (RNAi) therapy directed at ALK7, a receptor involved in fat-cell signalling. It is being tested in adults with obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes. It is not approved for any use.
The sole source of public information is a clinical trial registration: a Phase 1/2 first-in-human study (NCT06937203) that began on 9 May 2025, is recruiting, and plans to enroll 150 adults. No results have been reported in the sources reviewed.

name: WVE-007

chain: Fat cells break down more fat
angle.text: WVE-007 is an experimental siRNA that body-composition enthusiasts follow because its stated goal is losing visceral fat while preserving lean mass. Evidence so far is early company data; its effect on appearance has not been studied in published trials.

summary: An experimental liver-targeted siRNA aimed at cutting visceral fat while sparing muscle; early company data only, not approved.
note: Investigational; results are interim company-reported figures.
currentQuick:
WVE-007 is an experimental siRNA drug from Wave Life Sciences that silences the INHBE gene in the liver to lower Activin E. The aim is to reduce visceral fat while keeping lean mass.
The company has reported early single-dose results with visceral fat reductions, but these are interim and not independently confirmed.
How it works: A sugar tag (GalNAc) carries the siRNA to liver cells, where it shuts down INHBE production. Lower Activin E is thought to let fat cells break down more triglyceride.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse events in the early trial were mild or moderate, per the company. Long-term safety is unknown and the drug is not approved.
deepLead:
WVE-007 is an investigational GalNAc-conjugated small interfering RNA (siRNA) developed by Wave Life Sciences for obesity. It is designed to silence INHBE messenger RNA in the liver, lowering circulating Activin E, a liver-secreted protein that is described as restraining fat breakdown in fat cells. The stated goal is preferential loss of visceral fat while preserving lean mass.
According to company results summarised on Grokipedia, a single-dose Phase 1 cohort of adults with overweight or obesity showed dose-dependent Activin E suppression and, at six months after one dose, placebo-adjusted reductions in visceral fat, with lean mass stable or slightly higher. These are interim company-reported figures from a small early trial and have not been confirmed by peer-reviewed publication in the sources reviewed. The drug is not approved.
Grokipedia is AI-generated and its account should be treated with caution; the clinical trial registration is the verifiable record.

name: ALN-6222

angle.text: ALN-6222 is an experimental RNAi drug aimed at INHBE, a gene tied to fat distribution, and is followed by fat-loss readers as a possible next-generation obesity therapy. It has only just entered its first trial, so its appearance effects are untested.

summary: An experimental INHBE-targeting RNAi drug that has just entered its first obesity trial; nothing is known about results.
note: Investigational only; no published human data.
currentQuick:
ALN-6222 is an experimental RNA interference drug aimed at the INHBE gene and is in an early Phase 1 trial for obesity.
No results exist yet.
How it works: RNAi drugs lower production of a chosen protein by silencing its gene; the target here is INHBE.
Risks and caveats: No safety data have been reported. The drug is investigational and not available by prescription.
deepLead:
ALN-6222 is an investigational RNA interference (RNAi) therapy that targets INHBE, a gene linked to fat distribution, in people with obesity. It is not approved for any use.
Its only public footprint in the sources reviewed is a Phase 1 trial registration (NCT07624071), which started on 4 June 2026, is recruiting, and plans to enroll 88 participants. No results have been reported.

name: Monlunabant

angle.text: Monlunabant is an experimental oral CB1 blocker that fat-loss followers watch as a possible pill alternative to GLP-1 injections. Phase 2 showed modest weight loss with some neuropsychiatric side effects; its use for appearance beyond obesity treatment is untested.

summary: An experimental oral CB1 blocker for weight loss that showed modest results and some neuropsychiatric side effects in Phase 2.
note: Investigational; same drug class as rimonabant, withdrawn over psychiatric effects.
currentQuick:
Monlunabant is an experimental pill that blocks the CB1 receptor to reduce appetite and improve metabolism. It was designed to work mostly outside the brain.
A 16-week Phase 2a trial reported modest weight loss, and it is not approved anywhere.
How it works: It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor tied to appetite and energy balance. A 2025 study suggests part of its appetite effect is central.
Risks and caveats: The Phase 2a trial reported higher rates of mild to moderate anxiety and sleep disturbance than placebo; suicidal ideation was not reported. The earlier drug in this class, rimonabant, was withdrawn over psychiatric effects.
deepLead:
Monlunabant (also INV-202, MRI-1891) is an investigational, peripherally selective cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1) inverse agonist developed for obesity and metabolic disease. It was discovered by researchers at the US National Institutes of Health and developed by Inversago Pharma, and is now associated with Novo Nordisk. It is not approved for any use.
It belongs to a class whose first member, rimonabant, was approved in Europe in 2006 and withdrawn in 2008-2009 over psychiatric adverse events. Monlunabant was designed to act mostly outside the brain to reduce such effects. A Phase 2a trial in adults with obesity and metabolic syndrome reported weight loss described as modest, together with mild to moderate neuropsychiatric effects such as anxiety and sleep disturbance; suicidal ideation was not reported.

name: CRB-913

angle.text: CRB-913 is an experimental CB1 blocker followed by fat-loss readers as a possible add-on to GLP-1 drugs. It boosted weight loss in obese mice; human data are not yet public, so appearance use is untested.

summary: An experimental CB1 blocker that boosted GLP-1 drugs in obese mice; human data are not yet public.
note: Investigational; mouse data only published so far.
currentQuick:
CRB-913 is an experimental drug that blocks the CB1 receptor, with the aim of aiding weight loss. In mice it added to the effects of GLP-1-type drugs.
A Phase 1b human trial is listed as completed, but no results have been found.
How it works: It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor linked to appetite and metabolism, and is described as peripherally acting.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data are not public. The earlier CB1 blocker rimonabant was withdrawn over psychiatric effects; whether CRB-913 shares them is untested in published work.
deepLead:
CRB-913 is an investigational peripherally acting cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1) inverse agonist being studied for obesity. It is not approved for any use.
In a 2023 paper in Obesity, researchers reported that in diet-induced obese mice it enhanced the weight-loss efficacy of tirzepatide, semaglutide and liraglutide. A Phase 1b trial in otherwise healthy participants with obesity (NCT07310901, 254 participants, started December 2025) is registered as completed. No human results were identified in the sources reviewed.
